extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters and fiction writers (writers of dramatic scenes for film and prose)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing emotionally truthful, well-paced dramatic scenes (especially for cinema) by creating gaps between expectation and result, escalating risk, and writing from inside a character's point of view to elicit vivid reactions. Emphasizes beat-by-beat construction toward a turning point and avoidance of pacing/expository mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The gap between expectation and result
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance of story is the gap that splits open between what a human being expects to happen when he takes an action and what really does happen; the rift between expectation and result, probability and necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'gap' is the nexus of story and the source of its energy: it produces the audience's 'Oh, my God!' moments. To build a scene, constantly break open breaches between anticipation and outcome so the audience experiences surprise, revelation, or shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk: stakes must be meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure of the value of any human desire is in direct proportion to the risk involved in its pursuit; the higher the value, the higher the risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What is the risk? What's the worst thing that will happen to the protagonist if he does not achieve his desire? If failure merely returns life to normal, the story is misconceived. Stakes must threaten something genuinely valuable (time, money, relationships, freedom, life, soul).

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression of escalating risk and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a gap opens, the character must take a second, more difficult and risk-taking action; each action provokes antagonism and opens a new, larger gap, demanding still greater willpower and risk until a final action beyond which the audience cannot imagine another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the scene/story as a progression: each attempt increases jeopardy and demands deeper resources from the protagonist, building to a final, climax action.

rubrics_metrics.name: True action vs mere activity
rubrics_metrics.description: True action is physical, vocal, or mental movement that opens gaps in expectation and creates significant change. Mere activity is behavior in which what is expected happens, generating either no change or trivial change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer actions that split open reality (create surprising reactions). Avoid 'activity' that results in predictable, non-insightful outcomes; such moments are 'pointless pace killers' and should be cut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write from the inside out (Stanislavski's 'Magic If')
rubrics_metrics.description: The only reliable source of emotional truth is yourself: ask 'If I were this character in these circumstances, what would I do?' and act the role in your imagination until character-specific emotions flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not stay outside the character (which yields cliches). Using 'magic if' produces honest, specific emotion. Many great playwrights/screenwriters were actors; writers should improvise and perform their characters mentally to create authentic reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift points of view to pry open the gap
rubrics_metrics.description: After creating an honest moment from one point of view, move around your universe—to another character's POV or even the inanimate—and create an unexpected reaction that splinters the cleft between expectation and result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate subjective immersion (inside a character) with objective examination. Ask 'What is the opposite of that?' to invent a reaction the audience won't expect; then return to the first character under the new circumstances to find the next honest reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize reactions and insight over mere events
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine writing puts less stress on what happens than on to whom it happens and why and how it happens; the richest pleasures are found in stories that focus on the reactions that events cause and the insight gained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if genre conventions deliver predictable events (lovers meet, detective discovers crime), make interest by dramatizing how characters are affected and what is learned. Beat-by-beat emotional reaction matters more than plot tick-boxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat-by-beat construction toward a Turning Point
rubrics_metrics.description: Build scenes as a dynamic series of action → reaction → gap, renewed action → surprising reaction → gap, beat after beat, to and around the scene's Turning Point as reactions amaze and fascinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work the scene microscopically—what actors call 'inner monologues'—so that minutes on screen are generated from days at the desk. Each beat should advance emotional truth and escalate stakes toward the turning point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cliches, moralizing, 'cute' cleverness and guessing from outside
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions like 'How should someone take this action?' lead to cliches and moralizing; 'How might someone do this?' leads to 'cute'-clever but dishonest writing; 'If my character were in these circumstances, what would he do?' puts distance and yields guesses/cliches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'If I were this character...' (inside-out) to produce specific, honest behavior. Avoid writing from distance, which generates clichés and superficial characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid expository rewrites that weaken dramatic power
rubrics_metrics.description: Long explanatory exposition may slow the pace and weaken an antagonist by giving him sympathetic vulnerability or by resolving tension prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Chinatown example: replacing heavy backstory exposition with a brief, powerful exchange ('He raped you?') preserved antagonist cruelty and increased dramatic tension. Trim exposition that undermines the scene's energy or masks core conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'pointless pace killers' (dead seconds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes in which reactions lack insight and imagination—where expectation equals result—are 'pointless pace killers' and should be cut (editors will remove them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a beat delivers predictable, trivial reaction (e.g., character knocks and is politely admitted), skip to the next meaningful beat. Every moment must either reveal character, escalate stakes, or produce insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inner monologue to render moment-to-moment emotional truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting inner monologues on the page (ultra-slow motion of a scene) maps the flights of feeling and flashes of insight that create emotional truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when not printed, writers should perform inner monologues at the desk to discover honest impulses, sensory details, and emotional beats that make the scene vivid to readers/audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubt appearances; seek contradiction and the unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers are dialectical thinkers: the spirit of creation is contradiction—the breakthrough of appearances toward an unknown reality. Don't skim surfaces; peel back life to find the hidden and seemingly inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively ask 'What is the opposite of that?' and invent reactions that contradict expectations. Surprising, contradictory reactions are fertile sources of truth and drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your universe and use multiple perspectives (including inanimate)
rubrics_metrics.description: You are the God of your universe: know your characters, their minds, bodies, emotions, relationships, and world. Move around your universe—even into the inanimate—looking for points of view to invade and create unexpected reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep knowledge of the fictional world allows believable, specific reactions from varied perspectives. Use non-human/ambient viewpoints if they produce a useful gap or reveal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make writing vivid so readers 'live through' the gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Write vivid descriptions of what happens and the reactions it gets so that when someone else reads your pages he will, beat by beat, gap by gap, live through the roller coaster of life you lived through at your desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words are a means, not an end: make them lucid and sensory so the reader's pulse pounds, emotions flow, and meaning emerges. The page must allow the reader/audience to plunge into each gap and feel what you felt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story substance and energy derive from the gap (central evaluative test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stuff of a story is not its words but the gap between expectation and result; likewise, the source of energy in story is the gap that opens for character and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a scene or story, ask whether it creates and exploits such gaps; if not, it lacks substance and dramatic energy.
